steps.title: One stack for everyone
steps.caption: Everyone shares one stack. J's poison request and its retries crash every instance: 100% are hit.
steps.body: Twelve customers share one stack: one load balancer, eight app instances and one database. Customer J sends a **poison request**, one that crashes whichever instance handles it, and each retry crashes another until the service is down for everyone. A bad deployment would do the same, since it reaches every customer at once, and the only way to grow is to make this one stack bigger.

steps.title: Split into cells
steps.caption: Four identical cells share nothing. The router looks up each customer's cell and sends it there.
steps.body: The same stack is deployed as four identical, independent **cells**, each with its own load balancer, instances and database, and each serving a fixed list of customers. A thin **cell router** reads the request's partition key (here the customer ID), looks up that customer's cell and forwards the request, with no business logic of its own. Cells share no state and never call each other, so a failure inside one cell has no way into another.

steps.title: Failure stays in one cell
steps.caption: The poison request crashes only cell 2: 25% of customers. New versions go out one wave at a time.
steps.body: J's poison request is routed to cell 2, where it and its retry crash both instances, but only cell 2's customers D, J and M are affected: **25%** with four cells. K and the other customers of cells 1, 3 and 4 notice nothing. Cells contain bad deployments the same way: a new version goes to one cell first, bakes while its alarms are watched, and reaches the others only if it stays healthy.

steps.title: Grow by adding cells
steps.caption: Full cells stay at their tested size: a fifth cell takes the new customers. The router stays tiny.
steps.body: Each cell has a fixed maximum size that has been load-tested (here, three customers). When the cells are full, a fifth cell is added for the new customers instead of growing the old ones, and one cell's share of customers drops to 20%. The router is the one part every request passes through, so it stays a tiny lookup, runs replicated with its table cached in memory, and is changed with more care than any cell. Moving an existing customer to another cell means moving their data, so plan for it from the start.
